title: One reading for all
hookLine: Uthman sends standard copies of the Qur'an to the cities to unite the reading

cards: A soldier comes home from the far frontier, and what troubles him is not the enemy. It's his own side. The man is Hudhayfah ibn al-Yaman, and Bukhari tells what he saw on campaign in the north.

Muslims from Syria and Muslims from Iraq were serving together, and when they recited the Qur'an, they recited it differently, and they argued about it. Hudhayfah rides to Medina and goes straight to Uthman.
Commander of the faithful, he says, in effect, save this community before it divides over its own book.

teach.b: Bukhari's report is short and practical. Uthman sends to Hafsah, the Prophet's widow and Umar's daughter, who keeps the sheets of the Qur'an gathered in Abu Bakr's time, and borrows them.

teach.h: ZAYD COPIES IN THE SPEECH OF QURAYSH.
teach.b: He gives the work to Zayd ibn Thabit, who had written revelation for the Prophet, with men of Quraysh, and tells them: where you differ with Zayd over how a word is written, write it in the speech of Quraysh, because the Qur'an came down in their tongue.
They copy the sheets into books. The sheets go back to Hafsah.
A copy goes out to each province, with an order that other written collections be burned. That may startle a modern listener.
The tradition reads it as the opposite of disrespect: one agreed text, so no one would fight over private copies with their own additions and gaps.

Reports say Ali, asked about it later, defended what Uthman did with the copies. Muslims call a written copy a mushaf, and the standard copies are remembered as Uthman's. The Qur'an speaks of who keeps it.
In Pickthall's translation: "Lo! We, even We, reveal the Reminder, and lo! We verily are its Guardian." Tradition reads Uthman's work as one way that promise was carried out by human hands.
And the different ways of reciting were not erased: recognized recitations, the qira'at, are still learned and recited.
Unity of the written text, not one single voice.

how: Muslims call a written copy of the Qur'an a mushaf and commonly keep it in a clean, raised place; printed copies today follow the written text remembered as Uthman's, and recognized recitations are still taught.

games.q: one reading for all — tap the pairs.

s: Uthman wrote a new Qur'an of his own
Bukhari reports the copies were made from the sheets Hafsah kept, gathered in Abu Bakr's time.
the alarm came from a soldier on campaign
Hudhayfah ibn al-Yaman saw Muslims from Syria and Iraq arguing over recitation.
one written text means only one way of reciting survived
recognized recitations, the qira'at, are still learned and recited.

games.q: you're Uthman. armies are arguing over how the Qur'an is recited. what do you do?
o: let each city keep its own copies.
borrow Hafsah's sheets and send agreed copies to the provinces.
forbid reciting until the arguing stops.
games.why: Bukhari reports he borrowed the sheets, had Zayd and men of Quraysh copy them, and sent a copy to each province.

practice: Look at where your Qur'an sits, on a high shelf or under a coffee cup; if you don't have one, choose any book that matters to you, a scripture, a family Bible, a grandparent's letters.
Notice its weight, its wear, the hands it has passed through. If you can, move it somewhere cleaner and higher, or simply wipe the cover.

wordCard.voice: Mushaf, a written copy of the Qur'an: Uthman's standard copies, made from Hafsah's sheets and sent to the provinces, so the community would share one written text. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: a written copy of the Qur'an, bound between covers.

carryVoice: Your line: one text for all. A shared page can settle what memory can't. Day eight hundred seventy-eight, done.
